facts.name_origin: From the Spanish word montaña, meaning 'mountain' or 'mountainous country.'

government.chambers: Montana Senate (50 senators, 4-year terms) and Montana House of Representatives (100 representatives, 2-year terms)
government.executive: Governor (4-year term), who holds the executive power and sees that the laws are carried out; other elected executive officers are the lieutenant governor, secretary of state, attorney general, superintendent of public instruction, and auditor.
government.courts: Montana Supreme Court (a chief justice and six associate justices, elected statewide for 8-year terms), with district courts below it.
government.constitution: Current constitution written by a convention and ratified in 1972 (it replaced the 1889 statehood constitution). It is the only state constitution that commits the state to preserving the cultural integrity of American Indian peoples, which led to Indian Education for All.
government.kid_line: "The dignity of the human being is inviolable. No person shall be denied the equal protection of the laws." (Montana Constitution, Article II, Section 4)

long_ago.about: Their homeland is western Montana, where archaeologists have found sites showing people lived there continuously as far back as 12,600 years ago. They followed the seasons: digging bitterroot in spring and camas bulbs in June, hunting buffalo in summer when the wild rose bloomed, and fishing for trout through the winter.

The Ksanka Band of the Ktunaxa lived in the northwest mountains and lakes, traveling by season, fishing with weirs, and building light canoes for fast rivers. They grew their own kind of tobacco to use and trade, and their language is not related to any other language in the world.

long_ago.nation: Blackfeet (Piegan, part of the Niitsitapi or Blackfoot Confederacy)
long_ago.about: Blackfeet ancestors lived in present-day Saskatchewan until about 1730, then moved southwest where buffalo were plentiful. Horses changed their way of life, and they became powerful buffalo hunters on the northern plains east of the Rocky Mountains.

Crow ancestors once lived in earth-lodge villages on the Missouri River with the Hidatsa. Nearly 400 years ago one group, the Apsáalooke, moved west and claimed most of what is now eastern Montana and northern Wyoming, traveling as the Mountain Crow, River Crow, and Kicked in the Bellies.

The Ɔɔ’ɔɔɔ’niiinen’, the White Clay People, and the Nakoda traveled long distances on the northern plains following the buffalo, which gave them food, shelter, and tools. 'Assiniboine' comes from a name meaning 'ones who cook with stones,' for their way of boiling food with fire-heated rocks.

The Northern Cheyenne fought at the Little Bighorn in 1876. After being sent to Oklahoma, a northern group led by chiefs including Dull Knife returned to Montana, and Chief Dull Knife College on their reservation is named for him.

today.about: Blackfeet Reservation in northwestern Montana along the eastern slopes of the Rocky Mountains; Browning is the headquarters town.
Crow Reservation, about 2.2 million acres in south-central Montana; Crow Agency is the seat of the tribal government.
Flathead Reservation in western Montana, home of the Bitterroot Salish, Pend d'Oreille, and Kootenai.
Fort Belknap Reservation in north-central Montana, home to the Ɔɔ’ɔɔɔ’niiinen’ (Gros Ventre) and Nakoda (Assiniboine).

today.nation: Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes of Fort Peck
today.about: Fort Peck Reservation in northeastern Montana, home to bands of Nakoda (Assiniboine), Dakota, and Lakota.
Northern Cheyenne Reservation in southeastern Montana; Lame Deer is its main town.
Rocky Boy's Reservation, set aside in 1916 for the Chippewa and Cree bands of Chief Rocky Boy and Chief Little Bear.
Has no reservation; recognized by the state and federally recognized in December 2019.

first_peoples.today_note: Montana is home to twelve tribal nations (Assiniboine, Blackfeet, Chippewa, Cree, Crow, Gros Ventre, Kootenai, Little Shell Chippewa, Northern Cheyenne, Pend d'Oreille, Salish, and Sioux) with eight tribal governments: seven reservations plus the Little Shell Chippewa Tribe. Many Native people also live in cities such as Missoula, Billings, Great Falls, Butte, and Helena.
sites: First Peoples Buffalo Jump State Park near Great Falls: a mile-long sandstone cliff, possibly the largest bison cliff jump in North America, used for at least 1,000 years before Lewis and Clark.
Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument at Crow Agency, where Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors defeated the 7th Cavalry in 1876.
Chief Plenty Coups State Park near Pryor, on the Crow Reservation: the log home, sacred spring, and farm of the last traditional Crow chief.
Bear Paw Battlefield (Nez Perce National Historical Park) near Chinook, where Chief Joseph and the Nez Perce stopped fighting in 1877, about 40 miles from Canada.

history.event: Archaeological sites in the Salish and Pend d'Oreille homeland show people living in western Montana continuously since at least this time, soon after the glaciers melted back.
Native peoples begin using the cliff at today's First Peoples Buffalo Jump, driving bison over a mile-long sandstone cliff. Up to 18 feet of bison remains lie below it.
Blackfeet ancestors begin moving southwest from present-day Saskatchewan, following the buffalo onto the northern plains.

The Lewis and Clark expedition camps at Three Forks, where the Jefferson, Madison, and Gallatin rivers form the Missouri. Sacagawea, a young Native woman who had been captured near there as a child, traveled with them. So did York, a Black man enslaved by William Clark, the first Black person recorded in what became Montana. After the trip, Clark refused York's request for freedom for years.

The first Fort Laramie Treaty sets aside 33 million acres for the Crow Nation and a huge area for the Blackfeet, who were not consulted. Later treaties and acts of Congress shrank these lands again and again.
Prospectors find gold at Grasshopper Creek (July 28), starting Montana's gold rush at Bannack. Richer gold at Alder Gulch soon draws miners to Virginia City.
Congress creates Montana Territory, with Bannack as the first territorial capital.

On January 23, U.S. soldiers under Major Eugene Baker attack the wrong camp, the peaceful Piegan (Blackfeet) band of Chief Heavy Runner on the Marias River. At least 173 people, mostly women and children, are killed. This is called the Marias, or Baker, Massacre.

On June 25 and 26, Lakota, Northern Cheyenne, and Arapaho warriors defeat the U.S. Army's 7th Cavalry at the Battle of the Little Bighorn. The Army was trying to force them onto reservations after gold seekers invaded the Black Hills.

Nez Perce families fleeing the Army on a 1,300-mile journey are attacked at Big Hole and Bear Paw. On October 5, about 40 miles short of Canada, Chief Joseph agrees to stop fighting; about 150 Nez Perce escape to Canada.
With the buffalo nearly gone, the Blackfeet suffer failed hunts and starvation and are forced to depend on government rations on the reservation.
Montana becomes the 41st state on November 8.

trailblazers.name: Plenty Coups (Aleek-chea-ahoosh)
trailblazers.text: Plenty Coups, whose name means 'many achievements,' became a Crow chief by age 28. In 1884 he became one of the first Crow people to own and farm his own land near Pryor, where he ran a store. He and his wife, Strikes the Iron, gave their land to become a public park, and the Crow people named him their last traditional chief.

trailblazers.name: Charlo (Slem-hak-kah, 'Little Claw of a Grizzly Bear')
trailblazers.text: Born in the Bitterroot Valley, Chief Charlo never signed the 1872 agreement to move his people north, even though published copies showed his mark. He and several hundred Salish stayed in their Bitterroot homeland for about 20 more years, arguing for their right to a home there. In October 1891, as his people kept suffering, he reluctantly led them on a three-day journey to the Flathead Reservation.

trailblazers.name: Mary Fields
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved in Tennessee, Mary Fields came to St. Peter's Mission in Montana in 1885 and later lived in Cascade, where she was the only Black resident. In 1895 she won a contract to carry the U.S. mail by stagecoach on a 34-mile round trip, using snowshoes when the snow was too deep. She was the first African American woman to receive a Star Route mail contract.

trailblazers.name: Taylor Gordon (Emmanuel Taylor Gordon)
trailblazers.group: Black American man, singer and author
trailblazers.text: Born in White Sulphur Springs, Taylor Gordon worked as a chauffeur and railroad car chef before moving to New York, where he became part of the Harlem Renaissance. From 1925 he sang spirituals with pianist Rosamond Johnson, touring as far as Europe, and his life story, Born to Be, was published in 1929. He returned to White Sulphur Springs, where he died in 1971.

trailblazers.name: Jeannette Rankin
trailblazers.text: Born near Missoula, Rankin worked for women's right to vote, and Montana women won it in 1914. In 1916 she became the first woman elected to the U.S. Congress, four years before most American women could vote. She voted against entering both World War I and World War II because she believed war was not the way to solve conflicts.

trailblazers.name: Rose Hum Lee
trailblazers.text: Born in Butte to a Chinese merchant family, Rose Hum Lee earned a doctorate in sociology. In 1956 at Roosevelt University in Chicago she became the first woman and the first Chinese American to head a sociology department in America. Her research is one of the most important records of Chinese families in Montana.

trailblazers.name: Elouise Cobell (Yellow Bird Woman)
trailblazers.text: Born on the Blackfeet Reservation, Cobell founded the Blackfeet National Bank, the first national bank on a reservation owned by a tribe. She led a lawsuit proving the U.S. government had mismanaged money owed to more than 500,000 Native Americans, which ended in a $3.4 billion settlement and a scholarship fund. She was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016.

landforms: Rocky Mountains in the west, split by the Continental Divide
Northern Great Plains prairie covering about 60 percent of the state
Island mountain ranges rising out of the prairie, such as the Crazy Mountains
Granite Peak in the Beartooth Mountains, the highest point (12,799 feet)
Badlands in the east, such as Makoshika State Park
waters: Missouri River, which begins at Three Forks where the Jefferson, Madison, and Gallatin rivers meet
Flathead Lake, the largest natural freshwater lake in the western United States
Rivers in Glacier National Park that flow north toward Hudson Bay
geography.regions: The Continental Divide splits Montana into a mountainous west, part of the northern Rocky Mountains, and a drier eastern prairie that is part of the Great Plains.

ecosystems.name: Mountain forests and alpine meadows (Glacier National Park)
ecosystems.about: Glacier holds one of the largest grizzly bear populations in the lower 48 states. Bighorn sheep climb steep alpine slopes, and Canada lynx hunt snowshoe hares, which make up 60 to 97 percent of their diet.

ecosystems.name: Northern Great Plains prairie
ecosystems.about: Grasslands that once fed huge buffalo herds; black-tailed prairie dogs live in a town at First Peoples Buffalo Jump. In 2013 the Fort Belknap Indian Community released 34 genetically pure bison onto reservation prairie.

ecosystems.name: Cold rivers and lakes
ecosystems.about: Montana's rivers hold trout, including the state fish, the blackspotted cutthroat trout. The Salish and Pend d'Oreille fished for bull trout, cutthroat trout, and whitefish all year.

science.weather: Montana's winters can be bitterly cold; the east sometimes drops below -30°F, and blizzards are most common in the northeast. Warm chinook winds can raise temperatures very fast: at Loma on January 14 and 15, 1972, the temperature rose from -54°F to 49°F, a 103-degree change in 24 hours that is the official U.S. record. Yearly precipitation ranges from less than 7 inches in lowland valleys to more than 35 inches in the mountainous northwest. Drought brings wildfire: in 2012 more than 2,000 fires burned more than 1.2 million acres.
science.resources: Cattle ranching and farming have been central to Montana's economy since the 1850s, along with lumber and mining (gold, silver, coal, talc, and vermiculite). Tourism to Glacier and Yellowstone national parks is also important.
science.highlight: Glaciers: Glacier National Park's glaciers reached their largest size around 1850. USGS scientists found the number of glaciers bigger than 0.1 square kilometer dropped by nearly 60 percent from then until 2005, when only 32 remained. Montana is also a dinosaur state: its state fossil is Maiasaura, and the Hell Creek Formation is a major source of dinosaur fossils.

g3_ss.title: Montana's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Helena, Billings, and the seven reservations on a map; learn the three branches (Legislature, Governor, Supreme Court) and that tribal nations have their own governments too.

g3_ss.title: Montana's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the twelve tribal nations of Montana through the seasonal round of the Salish (bitterroot, camas, buffalo, fish) and a visit to First Peoples Buffalo Jump.

g3_ss.title: Montana Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Short biographies and timeline cards for Plenty Coups, Charlo, Mary Fields, Taylor Gordon, Jeannette Rankin, Rose Hum Lee, and Elouise Cobell; students write how each person changed their community.

g45_ss.title: Montana's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Compare Plateau nations (Salish, Pend d'Oreille, Ktunaxa) and Plains nations (Blackfeet, Crow, Gros Ventre, Nakoda, Northern Cheyenne): homelands, food, travel, and languages, using Montana's constitutional promise in Article X.

g45_ss.title: Explorers, Fur, and Gold
g45_ss.plan: Lewis and Clark at Three Forks told through Sacagawea and York (an enslaved man who asked for his freedom), the 1851 Fort Laramie Treaty, and the 1862 gold rush at Bannack and Virginia City.

g45_ss.title: Montana Territory to Statehood, 1864–1889
g45_ss.plan: Treaties and lost land, the Marias Massacre, Little Bighorn, the Nez Perce journey to Bear Paw, the end of the buffalo, and statehood as the 41st state, told from several perspectives.

g3_sci.title: Glaciers and Mountains
g3_sci.plan: What a glacier is, how Glacier National Park's glaciers have shrunk since 1850, and how meltwater feeds rivers; model a glacier with ice and sand.

g3_sci.title: Montana Dinosaurs
g3_sci.plan: Meet Maiasaura, the state fossil, and learn how fossils form in rock layers like the Hell Creek Formation.

g3_sci.title: Prairie Animals
g3_sci.plan: Food chains on the prairie: grasses, prairie dogs, bison, and predators; why bison returning to Fort Belknap matters.

g45_sci.title: Chinook Winds and Extreme Weather
g45_sci.plan: Use the Loma record (a 103-degree change in 24 hours) to explore air masses, rain shadows, and why western Montana is wetter than the east.

g45_sci.title: Glacier Change Data
g45_sci.plan: Graph USGS glacier counts in Glacier National Park and discuss what the trend shows about a warming climate and water supply.

g45_sci.title: Headwaters: Where the Missouri Begins
g45_sci.plan: Trace the Jefferson, Madison, and Gallatin to Three Forks and the Missouri; study watersheds, the Continental Divide, and trout habitat.
